title: Energy
question: How should the United States power homes, travel, and factories — and what should we do about cost, reliability, and pollution?
summary: Oil, gas, coal, nuclear, wind, solar, and water each keep the country running in a different way. This page will lay out the tradeoffs.
sourceNote: Further reading only. This outline does not take facts from these pages yet. When the full page is written, government or other primary sources will be cited first, and the Just Facts page will stay linked as further reading. The wording on this site will stay original. No statistics are included here.

paragraphs: This section will explain, in everyday words, where U.S. energy comes from and why the choice shows up in family bills, in whether the power stays on, and in pollution.
No statistics will be added until they are checked against primary sources.

This section will name the real disagreement: how to balance energy people can afford, a supply that does not flicker off, and air and climate that are safer. It will not treat either side as foolish.

sides.intro: Each column will hold one side’s strongest fair case, in plain language and at similar length. Neither case is written yet.

a.title: One side’s strongest case
paragraphs: This column will give the strongest fair case for one view, using checked facts. It will not use insults, and it is not written yet.

b.title: The other side’s strongest case
paragraphs: This column will give the strongest fair case for the other view, under the same rules. It is not written yet.
This section will name goals people on different sides often share, such as wanting energy families can count on, before it says where their plans still differ.

items: The questions will ask students to weigh cost, reliability, and pollution without pretending there is one obvious answer.
